System for physically transporting postcards, letters, and parcels. A postal service can be private or public, though many governments restrict private systems. Since the mid-19th century, national postal systems have generally been government monopolies, with the fee prepaid. Proof of payment is usually an adhesive [[Postage stamp|postage stamp]], though a postage meter is also used for bulk mailing. Some national authorities also run savings accounts and handle passport applications, and in some countries a postal, telegraph and telephone (PTT) service oversees telephone and telegraph systems as well. The Universal Postal Union, established in 1874, includes 192 member countries and sets the rules for international mail exchanges as a Specialized Agency of the [[United Nations]]. The United Kingdom introduced the adhesive stamp, the Penny Black, in 1840, shifting costs from recipients to senders.

The word comes from the [[Middle English]] *male*, a travelling bag or pack; by the 17th century it referred to a bag of letters, and later to the letters themselves. In the U.K. the Royal Mail delivers the "post," while in North America the U.S. Postal Service and Canada Post deliver the "mail." The term *email* first appeared in the 1970s.

The first documented organized courier service was in [[Egypt]], where pharaohs used couriers to send out decrees (2400 BC); the earliest surviving piece of mail, also Egyptian, dates to 255 BC. The first credible claim to a real postal system comes from the [[Achaemenid Empire]]. Xenophon attributes it to [[Cyrus the Great]] (550 BC), while others credit [[Darius the Great]] (521 BC), who rebuilt the Royal Road from Susa to Sardis. Couriers changed horses at stations called *Chapar Khaneh*. The model was adapted by the [[Roman Empire]] as the *cursus publicus*. In ancient India the Mauryan Empire (322–185 BC) developed an early mail service, and a postal system operated there by the end of the 18th century. In the United States, Benjamin Franklin became the first Postmaster General in 1775; rural free delivery began in 1896 and parcel post in 1913.

Tall, stout grass (*Zea mays*), also called corn, cultivated worldwide for its cereal grain. The leafy stalk bears male inflorescences, or tassels, that produce [[Pollen|pollen]], and female inflorescences called ears, which yield the grain, known as kernels. Plants range in height from 1.2 to 4 m, and kernels, arranged in 8 to 32 rows around the cob, are usually yellow or white in modern varieties but can be orange, red, brown, blue, purple, or black. Yellow maizes derive their color from [[Carotenoid|carotenoids]] and red maizes from [[Anthocyanin|anthocyanins]] and phlobaphenes.

Maize was domesticated by indigenous peoples in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago from wild teosinte. Native Americans planted it alongside beans and squashes in the Three Sisters polyculture. It relies on humans for its propagation. Since the [[Columbian exchange]], it has become a staple food in many parts of the world, and its total production surpasses that of wheat and rice. In 2020, world production was 1.1 billion tonnes. Much is used for animal feed; sweet corn is grown for human consumption, while field corn is made into cornmeal, masa, corn starch, corn syrup, corn oil, bourbon whiskey, and ethanol and other [[Biofuel|biofuels]]. Dishes include Mexican tortillas and tamales, Italian polenta, and American hominy grits. Maize protein is low in some essential amino acids, and its niacin becomes available only if freed by alkali treatment.

Maize is diploid with 20 chromosomes. [[Barbara McClintock]] used it to validate her transposon theory of "jumping genes," for which she won the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and it remains an important [[Model organism|model organism]] for genetics. The genome, sequenced by 2008, contains 32,540 genes. Two insect pests, European corn borer and corn rootworms, have each caused annual losses of a billion dollars in the United States. Much maize is now genetically modified.

Mosquito-borne infectious disease caused by single-celled parasites of the genus *Plasmodium*. It is transmitted by the bite of infected female *Anopheles* mosquitoes. The parasites first reproduce and mature in the [[Liver|liver]] without causing symptoms, then spread into the bloodstream, where they infect and destroy [[Red blood cell|red blood cells]]. Five species commonly infect humans. *P. falciparum*, responsible for the vast majority of deaths, *P. vivax*, and *P. knowlesi* are associated with more severe cases, while *P. ovale* and *P. malariae* generally cause milder illness.

Symptoms, which usually begin 10 to 15 days after the bite, include fever, chills, fatigue, vomiting, and headaches, and in severe cases [[Jaundice|jaundice]], seizures, [[Coma|coma]], or death. Without treatment, fever can recur every two or three days. Infected red blood cells can obstruct capillaries in vital organs; cerebral malaria, if untreated, can lead to death within forty-eight hours of the first symptoms. Survivors may develop partial immunity, which fades over months to years without continuing exposure. Diagnosis is by microscopic examination of blood films or rapid diagnostic tests; methods using the [[Polymerase chain reaction]] are considered the gold standard but are costly and not widely available where malaria is common.

Prevention relies on mosquito nets, repellents, insecticide spraying, draining standing water, and prophylactic medications. As of 2023, two malaria vaccines have been endorsed by the [[World Health Organization]]. Parasites have evolved resistance to several drugs: chloroquine-resistant *P. falciparum* has spread to most malaria-prone areas, and artemisinin resistance has become a problem in parts of [[Southeast Asia]].

The disease is widespread in a broad band of tropical and subtropical regions around the [[Equator|equator]]. In 2024, some 282 million cases resulted in an estimated 610,000 deaths. The WHO African Region accounted for approximately 94% of cases and 95% of deaths. Malaria is commonly associated with [[Poverty|poverty]]; in 2005 Africa was estimated to lose US$12 billion a year to it.

Austronesian pluricentric macrolanguage native to several islands of Maritime Southeast Asia and the Malay Peninsula. It is an official language of [[Brunei]], [[Malaysia]], and [[Singapore]], where the standardized forms are known as Standard Malay. Another standardized form, [[Indonesian language|Indonesian]], is the official language of [[Indonesia]] and one of the working languages of [[Timor-Leste]]. Malay is the ethnic language of Malays in Sumatra, Borneo, the Malay Peninsula, southeast Philippines, southern Thailand, and the Southern Province of Sri Lanka. About 80 million people speak it as a first language, and close to 300 million as a first or second language.

As a macrolanguage, it is a group of mutually intelligible speech varieties, a dialect continuum that may be considered distinct languages by their speakers. In Malaysia it is called either *Bahasa Melayu* or *Bahasa Malaysia*; in Indonesia the standard variety is *bahasa Indonesia*, while *bahasa Melayu* refers to vernacular varieties of central to southern Sumatra and West Kalimantan. Classical Malay, or Court Malay, was the literary standard of the Malacca and Johor Sultanates. Several Malay trade and creole languages, such as Ambonese Malay, derive from a lingua franca based on it.

Historical linguists place the Malayic homeland in western Borneo, where Proto-Malayic was spoken by at least 1000 BC. The history of Malay is divided into Old Malay, the Transitional Period, Classical Malay, Late Modern Malay, and Modern Malay. Old Malay was influenced by [[Sanskrit]], and its earliest known stone inscription, the Kedukan Bukit inscription found near [[Palembang]] on Sumatra, is dated May 1, 683. The maritime empire of [[Srivijaya]], based on Sumatra from the 7th to the 11th centuries, spread Old Malay across the Malay Peninsula and Archipelago, where it served as the lingua franca of traders. The traditional Jawi script, adapted from Arabic, persists alongside the Latin script.

Federal constitutional monarchy, Southeast Asia (pop., over 34 million). It consists of 13 states and three federal territories, separated by the [[South China Sea]] into Peninsular Malaysia on mainland Southeast Asia and East Malaysia on the island of [[Borneo]]. Peninsular Malaysia borders Thailand by land; East Malaysia shares land borders with [[Brunei]] and Indonesia. [[Kuala Lumpur]] is the national capital, largest city, and seat of the legislature; Putrajaya is the federal administrative capital. It is the world's 43rd-most populous country.

The country has its origins in the Malay kingdoms, which from the 18th century on became subject to the [[British Empire]]. During [[World War II]], British Malaya was occupied by the [[Empire of Japan]]. The Federation of Malaya, restructured in 1948, achieved independence on August 31, 1957. On September 16, 1963, it united with the British crown colonies of North Borneo, Sarawak, and [[Singapore]] to become Malaysia; Singapore separated and became independent in August 1965.

Malaysia is tropical and is one of 17 megadiverse countries. About half the population is ethnically Malay, with minorities of Chinese, Indians, and indigenous peoples. The Bumiputra policy grants the Malay majority a constitutionally enshrined privileged status through affirmative action; debates over it persist. The official language is Malaysian Malay, a standard form of the [[Malay language]], and English remains an active second language. The constitution recognizes [[Islam]] as the official religion and grants freedom of religion to non-Muslims, though conversion out of Islam is forbidden while conversion to it is allowed.

The government is modelled on the Westminster parliamentary system, and the legal system is based on common law. The head of state is an elected monarch chosen among the nine state rulers every five years; the head of government is the prime minister. The economy, once reliant on agriculture and primary commodities, is now driven by services and manufacturing. Malaysia is a founding member of [[ASEAN]] and also belongs to the Commonwealth of Nations and the Non-Aligned Movement.

Empire in West Africa, c. 1235 to 1610. Founded by Sundiata Keita, it became renowned for the wealth of its monarchs, especially [[Mansa Musa]]. At its peak it was the largest empire in West Africa, influencing the region's culture through the spread of its language, laws, and customs.

It began as a small Mandinka kingdom at the upper reaches of the [[Niger River]], centered on the Manding region, and developed during the 11th and 12th centuries as the [[Ghana Empire]] declined and trade shifted southward. Its early history is unclear because of conflicting accounts by Arab chroniclers and oral traditionalists. Sundiata Keita, a warrior-prince of the Keita dynasty, freed the local people from the king of the Sosso Empire, Soumaoro Kanté; the conquest of Sosso in c. 1235 marked Mali's emergence as a major power, with the Kouroukan Fouga as its constitution. After Sundiata's death in c. 1255, rulers bore the title *mansa*. In 1285, Sakura, a former slave of the imperial family who had risen to general, carried out a military coup, and the Keita line was restored with Mansa Gao.

Mansa Musa took the throne in c. 1312 and made a famous pilgrimage to [[Mecca]] from 1324 to 1326, where his gifts and expenditure of [[Gold|gold]] caused significant inflation in Egypt. Maghan I succeeded him in c. 1337 but was deposed by his uncle Suleyman in 1341. During Suleyman's 19-year reign [[Ibn Battuta]] visited Mali; his death marked the end of Mali's Golden Age and the start of a slow decline.

Mali remained a sizeable state in the 15th century. From 1507 neighboring states, including the [[Songhai Empire]], chipped away at its borders. In 1544–45 the Songhai invaded the capital but failed to conquer it. A disastrous defeat outside Djenne in 1599 ended hopes of recovery after Songhai's collapse, and the empire disintegrated into independent chiefdoms; the Keitas retreated to Kangaba as provincial chiefs. Much of the evidence comes from [[Ibn Khaldun]], Ibn Battuta, Leo Africanus, and Mandinka oral tradition kept by griots.

Vertebrate animal of the class Mammalia, characterized by milk-producing mammary glands for feeding the young, a broad neocortex region of the brain, fur or hair, and three middle ear bones. These traits distinguish mammals from reptiles and birds, from which their ancestors diverged in the Carboniferous period over 300 million years ago. About 6,640 extant species have been described and divided into 27 orders. The study of mammals is called mammalogy.

The largest orders by number of species are the [[Rodent|rodents]], [[Bat|bats]], and eulipotyphlans (hedgehogs, moles, and shrews), followed by the [[Primate|primates]], the even-toed ungulates (including pigs, bovids, and whales), and the [[Carnivora]]. Mammals are the only living members of the clade [[Synapsida]]. They originated from cynodonts, an advanced group of therapsids, during the Late Triassic to Early Jurassic, and achieved their modern diversity in the Paleogene and Neogene periods of the Cenozoic era, after the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs. They have been the dominant terrestrial animal group from 66 million years ago to the present.

The basic body type is quadrupedal, but limbs are adapted for life at sea, in the air, in trees, or underground. Mammals range in size from the 30–40 mm bumblebee bat to the 30 m [[Blue whale]], possibly the largest animal ever. Maximum lifespan varies from two years for the shrew to 211 years for the bowhead whale. All modern mammals give birth to live young except the five species of monotremes, which lay eggs. The most species-rich group is the placental mammals. Most are intelligent, and they communicate through ultrasound, scent marking, alarm signals, singing, and echolocation; in humans, through complex language.

Domestication of mammals played a major role in the [[Neolithic Revolution]], helping replace hunting and gathering with farming. Domesticated mammals supply power for transport and agriculture, as well as meat, dairy products, fur, and leather. The decline and extinction of many mammals is driven primarily by poaching and habitat destruction, chiefly deforestation.

Adult male human. Before adulthood, a male child or adolescent is called a boy. A man's genome usually inherits an X chromosome from the mother and a Y chromosome from the father, and sex differentiation of the male fetus is governed by the *SRY* gene on the Y chromosome. During [[Puberty|puberty]], hormones that stimulate androgen production produce secondary sexual characteristics, including greater muscle mass, greater height, facial hair growth, and lower body fat composition. Male anatomy is distinguished by the male reproductive system, which includes the testicles, sperm ducts, prostate gland, epididymides, and penis; secondary characteristics include a narrower pelvis and hips and smaller breasts and nipples. Men tend to be taller and heavier than women and, adjusted for height, to have greater lean and bone mass and lower fat mass.

The English word derives from Old English *mann*, which primarily meant "person" or "human being" and referred to men, women, and children alike; the distinct word for an adult male was *wer*, which survives today only in compounds such as "werewolf." *Mann* came to mean "man" in Middle English.

Throughout history, traditional gender roles have often defined masculinity and men's activities and opportunities, and many societies have been patriarchal, giving men considerable power, particularly over women. Men are over-represented as both perpetrators and victims of violence, are often directed into professions with high mortality rates, and are most often subject to conscription into military service. Many religious doctrines set rules for men, such as religious circumcision. Critiques of the impact of these roles have prompted movement toward [[Gender equality|gender equality]] and the diverse men's movement. Trans men have a gender identity that does not align with the female sex they were assigned at birth, while intersex men may have sex characteristics that do not fit typical notions of male biology.

Administration of organizations, whether businesses, nonprofit organizations, or government bodies, through business administration, nonprofit management, or public administration respectively. It is the process of managing the resources of businesses, governments, and other organizations.

Larger organizations generally have three hierarchical levels of managers. Senior management, including the board of directors and a chief executive officer (CEO) or president, sets strategic goals and policies and decides how the organization will operate. Middle management, including branch, regional, department, and section managers, directs front-line managers and communicates senior management's goals and policies to them. Line management, made up of supervisors and frontline managers or team leaders, oversees regular employees or volunteers and performs the functions traditionally considered the core of management, though line managers are usually considered part of the workforce rather than the management class.

The English verb derives from the fifteenth-century French *mesnager*, which referred in equestrian language to holding a horse's reins, and ultimately from the [[Latin]] *manus* (hand) and *agere* (to act). The noun dates to the 1590s. Definitions vary. Henri Fayol stated: "To manage is to forecast and to plan, to organize, to command, to co-ordinate and to control." Peter Drucker saw the basic task of management as twofold: marketing and innovation. Fredmund Malik defines it as "the transformation of resources into utility." Frederick Winslow Taylor's scientific management applied empirical analysis of workflows through time-motion studies to improve efficiency, and it also prompted debate over worker autonomy.

Management is taught as both theory and practice at colleges and universities, with prominent degree programs in management, business administration, and public administration. Social scientists study it as an academic discipline, investigating social organization, organizational adaptation, and organizational leadership. In recent decades there has been a movement for evidence-based management.

Ruler of the [[Mali Empire]] (r. c. 1312–c. 1337). The empire reached its territorial peak during his reign, which is often regarded as the zenith of Mali's power and prestige, although he features less in Mandinka oral traditions than his predecessors.

Contemporaries described Musa as inconceivably rich. His wealth came principally from the empire's control and taxing of the trade in salt from northern regions and especially from gold panned and mined in Bambuk and Bure to the south. It is estimated that two thirds of the gold circulating in the medieval Mediterranean came from West Africa. Archaeological work near Tadmekka suggests that Malians invented their own process of refining gold using melted glass. At his accession, Mali consisted largely of the territory of the former [[Ghana Empire]], which had become a vassal of Mali. The empire comprised land now in Guinea, Senegal, Mauritania, the Gambia, and modern Mali, an area of 1,300,000 km².

Musa went on the [[Hajj]] to Mecca in 1324, traveling with an enormous entourage and a vast supply of gold. In Cairo, his lavish gift-giving is said to have noticeably affected the value of gold in Egypt and drew the attention of the wider Muslim world. He expanded the empire's borders, incorporating the cities of Gao and [[Timbuktu]], and sought closer ties with the Mamluk and Marinid Sultanates. He recruited scholars from the wider Muslim world, such as the Andalusian poet Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, and helped establish Timbuktu as a center of Islamic learning. His reign is associated with numerous construction projects, including part of the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu.

Much of what is known about him comes from Arabic sources written after his pilgrimage, especially the writings of Al-Umari and [[Ibn Khaldun]], and from two 17th-century Timbuktu manuscripts, the *Tarikh Ibn al-Mukhtar* and the *Tarikh al-Sudan*.
